blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The Kruskal-Wallis test compares three or more independent groups. It ranks all observations together and tests whether the groups’ mean ranks differ more than chance would allow. It is the rank-based counterpart of one-way ANOVA (recall §9.5.2).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
It is the Mann-Whitney idea applied to k groups. Under H₀ every group’s mean rank should be close to the overall mean rank, (N + 1)/2. The statistic H adds up the squared distances of the group mean ranks from that centre, weighted by group size, and scales them so that H is approximately χ² with k − 1 degrees of freedom (recall §5.7.2.4).

H = [12 ÷ (N(N + 1))] × Σ nᵢR̄ᵢ² − 3(N + 1)

where nᵢ and R̄ᵢ are the size and mean rank of group i.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In the CBHI survey, does distance to the facility differ by maternal education (none, primary, secondary or higher)? Median distances are 9.0, 8.5 and 7.1 km.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Rank all 500 distances. Mean ranks: none 289.5 (n = 168), primary 263.3 (n = 177), secondary+ 193.6 (n = 155). The overall mean rank is 501/2 = 250.5.
  2. Σ nᵢR̄ᵢ² = 168 × 289.52² + 177 × 263.32² + 155 × 193.56² = 32,162,647.
  3. H = 12 ÷ (500 × 501) × 32,162,647 − 3 × 501 = 1,540.73 − 1,503 = 37.73, on k − 1 = 2 df.
  4. The 5% critical value of χ² with 2 df is 5.99. H far exceeds it (p < 0.001): distance differs across education groups.

Dunn’s post-hoc test. Like ANOVA, a significant H says only that at least one group differs. To find which, Dunn’s test (Dunn, 1964) compares each pair’s mean ranks using the pooled ranking from the Kruskal-Wallis test:

z = (R̄ᵢ − R̄ⱼ) ÷ √[S² × (1/nᵢ + 1/nⱼ)], with S² = N(N + 1)/12 (less a small correction for ties)

and then adjusts the p-values for the number of comparisons, for example by Bonferroni (recall §9.5.3). For none vs secondary+: S² = 500 × 501/12 = 20,875; z = (289.5 − 193.6) ÷ √[20,875 × (1/168 + 1/155)] = 95.9 ÷ 16.1 = 5.96.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cb <- read.csv("data/cbhi_survey.csv")
kruskal.test(distance_km ~ maternal_education, data = cb)
# Dunn's post-hoc test (base R): compare mean ranks pair by pair
r  <- rank(cb$distance_km); g <- factor(cb$maternal_education)
N  <- length(r); t <- table(cb$distance_km)
# rank variance, tie-corrected
S2 <- N * (N + 1) / 12 - sum(t^3 - t) / (12 * (N - 1))
Rm <- tapply(r, g, mean); n <- table(g)
pr <- combn(levels(g), 2)
z  <- apply(pr, 2, function(k)
  (Rm[k[1]] - Rm[k[2]]) / sqrt(S2 * (1/n[k[1]] + 1/n[k[2]])))
p  <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))
data.frame(pair = paste(pr[1, ], "vs", pr[2, ]), z = round(z, 2),
           p = signif(p, 3),
           p_bonferroni = signif(p.adjust(p, "bonferroni"), 3))

    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  distance_km by maternal_education
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 37.733, df = 2, p-value = 6.404e-09

                   pair    z        p p_bonferroni
1       none vs primary 1.68 9.23e-02     2.77e-01
2    none vs secondary+ 5.96 2.46e-09     7.37e-09
3 primary vs secondary+ 4.39 1.13e-05     3.40e-05

The first block is H = 37.73 on 2 df from step 3. Dunn’s table shows where the difference lies: secondary+ households live closer than both other groups (Bonferroni p < 0.001), while none and primary do not differ clearly (adjusted p = 0.28). The packages dunn.test and FSA do the same in one line.

points.html: Same assumptions as Mann-Whitney, for k groups; the same shape caveat applies to reading it as a comparison of medians.
With two groups, Kruskal-Wallis gives the same p-value as the Mann-Whitney test (without continuity correction), just as one-way ANOVA with two groups reproduces the t-test.
Use Dunn’s test (with a multiplicity adjustment) for pairwise follow-up, not repeated Mann-Whitney tests with separate rankings.
